claim: 14-3-3 interacts with spastin both in vivo and in vitro via spastin Ser233 phosphorylation.
source: Here, we use glutathione transferase pulldown and immunoprecipitation assays to demonstrate that 14-3-3 interacts with spastin, both in vivo and in vitro, via spastin Ser233 phosphorylation.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from GST pulldown and immunoprecipitation assays described in the abstract and detailed in the results section.

claim: 14-3-3 protects spastin from degradation by inhibiting the ubiquitination pathway.
source: Moreover, we show that 14-3-3 protects spastin from degradation by inhibiting the ubiquitination pathway and upregulates the spastin-dependent severing ability.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data including ubiquitination assays and protein stability experiments shown in Figure 3.

claim: 14-3-3 upregulates the spastin-dependent severing ability.
source: Moreover, we show that 14-3-3 protects spastin from degradation by inhibiting the ubiquitination pathway and upregulates the spastin-dependent severing ability.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing microtubule severing assays in COS7 cells (Figure 3P-Q).

claim: The 14-3-3 agonist Fusicoccin (FC-A) promotes neurite outgrowth and regeneration in vitro which needs spastin activation.
source: Furthermore, the 14-3-3 agonist Fusicoccin (FC-A) promotes neurite outgrowth and regeneration in vitro which needs spastin activation.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from hippocampal and cortical neuron cultures treated with FC-A and spastazoline (Figure 4).

claim: 14-3-3 protein is upregulated in the neuronal compartment after spinal cord injury in vivo.
source: Western blot and immunofluorescence results revealed that 14-3-3 protein is upregulated in the neuronal compartment after spinal cord injury in vivo.
evidence: The claim is supported by western blot and immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 5A-B.

claim: Administration of FC-A promotes locomotor recovery following spinal cord injury in both contusion and lateral hemisection models.
source: In addition, administration of FC-A not only promotes locomotor recovery, but also nerve regeneration following spinal cord injury in both contusion and lateral hemisection models; however, the application of spastin inhibitor spastazoline successfully reverses these phenomena.
evidence: The claim is supported by BMS scores, catwalk analysis, footprint tests, and MEP recordings shown in Figures 6 and 7.

claim: Administration of FC-A promotes nerve regeneration following spinal cord injury in both contusion and lateral hemisection models.
source: In addition, administration of FC-A not only promotes locomotor recovery, but also nerve regeneration following spinal cord injury in both contusion and lateral hemisection models; however, the application of spastin inhibitor spastazoline successfully reverses these phenomena.
evidence: The claim is supported by histological data including neurofilament and 5-HT staining shown in Figures 5 and 7.

claim: The application of spastin inhibitor spastazoline reverses the beneficial effects of FC-A on locomotor recovery and nerve regeneration after spinal cord injury.
source: In addition, administration of FC-A not only promotes locomotor recovery, but also nerve regeneration following spinal cord injury in both contusion and lateral hemisection models; however, the application of spastin inhibitor spastazoline successfully reverses these phenomena.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data comparing FC-A treatment alone versus FC-A plus spastazoline treatment in Figures 5, 6, and 7.

claim: Axon regeneration is abortive in the central nervous system following injury.
source: Axon regeneration is abortive in the central nervous system following injury.
evidence: This is a general statement about CNS injury that draws from established scientific knowledge in the field.

claim: Orchestrating microtubule dynamics has emerged as a promising approach to improve axonal regeneration.
source: Orchestrating microtubule dynamics has emerged as a promising approach to improve axonal regeneration.
evidence: This statement reflects current scientific understanding and research directions in the field of axonal regeneration.

claim: The microtubule severing enzyme spastin is essential for axonal development and regeneration through remodeling of microtubule arrangement.
source: The microtubule severing enzyme spastin is essential for axonal development and regeneration through remodeling of microtubule arrangement.
evidence: This statement is supported by references to previous studies and is consistent with established knowledge about spastin function.

claim: Regeneration of the adult central nervous system neurons is difficult after injury, a phenomenon that results in permanent neurological impairments.
source: Regeneration of the adult central nervous system neurons is difficult after injury, a phenomenon that results in permanent neurological impairments (Curcio and Bradke, 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Curcio and Bradke, 2018.

claim: Limited cell-intrinsic growth capacity contributes to the difficulty of CNS regeneration after injury.
source: Researchers have attributed this not only to the highly inhibitory extrinsic environment at the injury site but also to limited cell-intrinsic growth capacity.
evidence: This statement reflects established understanding in the field of CNS injury research.

claim: Re-programming of growth-associated processes plays a key role in manipulation of axonal regeneration.
source: Many studies have demonstrated that re-programming of growth-associated processes plays a key role in manipulation of axonal regeneration (Hilton et al., 2022; Mahar and Cavalli, 2018; Clark et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Hilton et al., 2022; Mahar and Cavalli, 2018; Clark et al., 2014.

claim: Cytoskeleton remodeling, including actin and microtubule reorganization, appears to be the key factors directing the fate of axonal regeneration and sprouting.
source: Cytoskeleton remodeling, including actin and microtubule (MT) reorganization, appears to be the key factors directing the fate of axonal regeneration and sprouting (Jin, 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Jin, 2015.

claim: The retraction bulb of severed axons at the lesion site of the spinal cord needs a dynamic cytoskeleton for successful regeneration.
source: Notably, the retraction bulb of severed axons at the lesion site of the spinal cord needs a dynamic cytoskeleton for successful regeneration.
evidence: This statement is based on established understanding of axonal injury and regeneration mechanisms.

claim: The formation of axon collaterals from spared axons needs dynamic cytoskeleton reorganization to form new neural circuits with the innervated neurons.
source: Moreover, the formation of axon collaterals from spared axons also needs dynamic cytoskeleton reorganization to form new neural circuits with the innervated neurons (Pinto-Costa et al., 2020; Crunkhorn, 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Pinto-Costa et al., 2020; Crunkhorn, 2015.

claim: Invasion by microtubules can provide mechanical force and guide intracellular transport to regulate distribution of specific molecules.
source: Mechanistically, invasion by MTs can not only provide mechanical force, but also guide intracellular transport to regulate distribution of specific molecules, including mitochondria, peroxisomes, growth factors and others, and subsequently mediate axonal extension.
evidence: This statement reflects established understanding of microtubule function in neurons.

claim: Timely invasion of microtubules can power the formation of a growth cone with competent growth ability from the retraction bulb.
source: Therefore, timely invasion of microtubules can not only power the formation of a growth cone with competent growth ability from the retraction bulb, but also improve the process of axonal sprouting from the spared axons (Chen and Rolls, 2012; Vargas et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Chen and Rolls, 2012; Vargas et al., 2020.

claim: Manipulating microtubule dynamics is critical for boosting axon regeneration.
source: Overall, manipulating MT dynamics is critical for boosting axon regeneration.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the preceding discussion and supported by the cited literature.

claim: Spastin is encoded by SPAST gene and its mutations was identified in patients with hereditary spastic paraplegia (HSP).
source: Spastin is encoded by SPAST gene and its mutations was identified in patients with hereditary spastic paraplegia (HSP) (Shribman et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Shribman et al., 2019.

claim: Spastin is a microtubule severing enzyme that can cut long microtubules into short fragments.
source: It is an MT severing enzyme (including spastin, katanin, and fidgetin) which can cut long MTs into short fragments, a phenomenon that not only endows MTs with high dynamics but also mediates their subsequent turning and regrowth under physiological conditions (Liu et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Liu et al., 2021.

claim: Spastin has two major isoforms, namely M1 and M87, coded from different translation initiation codons.
source: Spastin has two major isoforms, namely M1 and M87, coded form different translation initiation codons (1st and 87th methionine).
evidence: This is established knowledge about spastin protein structure.

claim: Both spastin isoforms (M1 and M87) are highly expressed in the spinal cord.
source: Both isoforms are highly expressed in the spinal cord (Salinas et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Salinas et al., 2007.

claim: SPAST mutation can lead to the degeneration of the corticospinal tracts in HSP patients.
source: Moreover, SPAST mutation can lead to the degeneration of the corticospinal tracts in HSP patients.
evidence: This is established clinical knowledge about hereditary spastic paraplegia.

claim: Spastin is highly expressed in the central neuronal system (CNS) and essential for formation of axon branches as well as their extension during neural development.
source: In addition, spastin is highly expressed in the central neuronal system (CNS) and essential for formation of axon branches as well as their extension during neural development (Lopes et al., 2020; Ji et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Lopes et al., 2020; Ji et al., 2020.

claim: Excess or deficient dosage of spastin is detrimental to axon regeneration in Drosophila.
source: Intriguingly, a study conducted in Drosophila has reported that excess or deficient dosage of spastin is detrimental to axon regeneration (Stone et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Stone et al., 2012.

claim: Spastin is significant in coordinating the concentration of the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) and microtubules at the growing axon tips during axon regeneration in Drosophila.
source: Furthermore, another study in Drosophila has also indicated the significance of spastin in coordinating the concentration of the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) and microtubules at the growing axon tips during axon regeneration (Rao et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Rao et al., 2016.

claim: Spastin conjugated with polyethylene glycol administered into the epineurium has potential in mediating the recovery of motor function following sciatic nerve injury.
source: In a separate study, researchers administered spastin conjugated with polyethylene glycol into the epineurium and observed its potential in mediating the recovery of motor function following sciatic nerve injury. However, this study lacks the requisite histological and molecular biological evidence (Lin et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Lin et al., 2019, but the authors note the study lacks comprehensive evidence.

claim: There is insufficient research to definitively establish the role of spastin in axon regeneration after central nervous system injury in adult mammals.
source: Currently, there is insufficient research to definitively establish the role of spastin in axon regeneration after central nervous system injury in adult mammals.
evidence: This is an assessment of the current state of the literature by the authors.

claim: Direct manipulation of the SPAST gene may not be the most appropriate approach for promoting successful axon regeneration after CNS injury due to dose-dependent effects.
source: Therefore, direct manipulation of the SPAST gene may not be the most appropriate approach for promoting successful axon regeneration after the CNS injury.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the discussion of dose-dependent effects of spastin.

claim: Post-translational modifications, protein metabolism, and protein-protein interactions are vital for regulating protein activity.
source: It is worth noting that post-translational modifications, protein metabolism, and protein-protein interactions are vital for regulating the protein's activity (Martins-Marques et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Martins-Marques et al., 2019.

claim: 14-3-3 protein is a type of adaptor protein that plays important roles in many signaling pathways through interaction with their substrates.
source: 14-3-3 protein is a type of adaptor protein that plays important roles in many signaling pathways through interaction with their substrates (Fu et al., 2021b; Fu et al., 2021a).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Fu et al., 2021b; Fu et al., 2021a.

claim: 14-3-3 inhibits ROS-induced cell death by interacting with FOXO transcription factors to prevent upregulation of many pro-apoptotic genes.
source: For instance, it inhibits the ROS-induced cell death by interacting with FOXO transcription factors to prevent upregulation of many pro-apoptotic genes (Nielsen et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Nielsen et al., 2008.

claim: In mammals, seven 14-3-3 isoforms have been identified: β, γ, ε, ζ, η, θ, and σ.
source: In mammals, seven isoforms, namely β,γ,ε,ζ,η,θ, and σ, have been identified.
evidence: This is established knowledge about 14-3-3 protein isoforms.

claim: 14-3-3 isoforms are highly conserved in the mammalian system and form a dimeric structure to interact with their substrates which are mostly phosphoproteins.
source: They are not only highly conserved in the mammalian system, but also form a dimeric structure to interact with their substrates which are mostly phosphoproteins (Park et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Park et al., 2019.

claim: Spastin is phosphorylated at Ser233 which showed its potential for interaction with 14-3-3.
source: Previous studies have shown that spastin is phosphorylated in Ser233 which showed its potential for interaction with 14-3-3 (Pisciottani et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Pisciottani et al., 2019.

claim: 14-3-3 protein is highly expressed in CNS where it plays a vital role in both axonal growth and guidance.
source: In addition, 14-3-3 protein is also highly expressed in CNS where it plays a vital role in both axonal growth and guidance.
evidence: This statement reflects established knowledge about 14-3-3 function in the nervous system.

claim: 14-3-3 promotes cortical neurite outgrowth and axon regeneration.
source: Previous studies have also demonstrated that 14-3-3 promotes cortical neurite outgrowth and axon regeneration (Kaplan et al., 2017; Yam et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Kaplan et al., 2017; Yam et al., 2012.

claim: 14-3-3 was identified as a putative spastin-interacting protein through GST-spastin pulldown assays and mass spectrometry analysis.
source: In our previous study (Ji et al., 2021), GST-spastin pulldown assays with proteins lysed from the spinal cord tissue were performed, and the obtained proteins were analyzed via mass spectrometry to determine the underlying molecular mechanisms of spastin. The peptides that interacted with GST were subtracted from those interacting with GST-spastin, and the peptides of proteins that interacts with spastin were obtained. We revealed 14-3-3 as putative spastin-interacting proteins (Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from GST pulldown and mass spectrometry shown in Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: 14-3-3 and spastin endogenously interact in the spinal cord tissue and cortical neurons.
source: Next, we employed immunoprecipitation to determine the biochemical interaction between 14-3-3 protein and spastin, and found that they endogenously interacted in the spinal cord tissue and the cortical neurons (Figure 1B and C).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 1B and C.

claim: 14-3-3 exhibits a characteristic distribution in axons, including aggregation at the growth cone and specific locations in the axon shaft.
source: The results revealed that 14-3-3 exhibited a characteristic distribution in axons, including aggregation at the growth cone and specific locations in the axon shaft, while spastin also showed accumulations at the sites where 14-3-3 proteins aggregated.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data from hippocampal neurons shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Spastin shows accumulations at the sites where 14-3-3 proteins aggregate in hippocampal neurons.
source: The results revealed that 14-3-3 exhibited a characteristic distribution in axons, including aggregation at the growth cone and specific locations in the axon shaft, while spastin also showed accumulations at the sites where 14-3-3 proteins aggregated.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data from hippocampal neurons shown in Figure 1D.

claim: All six tested 14-3-3 isoforms (β, γ, ε, ζ, η, θ) can interact with spastin in vitro.
source: Results from a GST pull-down assay revealed that all 14-3-3 isoforms could interact with spastin (Figure 1H).
evidence: The claim is supported by GST pulldown data shown in Figure 1H.

claim: All six tested 14-3-3 isoforms can form complexes with spastin in co-immunoprecipitation assays.
source: Subsequent co-immunoprecipitation assay results also confirmed that all 14-3-3 isoforms could form complexes with spastin (Figure 1I).
evidence: The claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 1I.

claim: Spastin fragments containing amino acids 85–316 but not those with 85–214 coprecipitate with 14-3-3.
source: Co-immunoprecipitation assay, using GFP-Trap beads, revealed that spastin fragments containing amino acids 85–316 but not those with 85–214 coprecipitated with 14-3-3 (Figure 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data using spastin deletion constructs shown in Figure 2B.

claim: 14-3-3 specifically binds to the region (215–336 amino acids) of spastin.
source: Next, we performed immunoprecipitation assays using the region (215–336 amino acids) of spastin with 14-3-3 and found that 14-3-3 specifically binds to the region (215–336 amino acids) of spastin (Figure 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Staurosporine significantly reduces the phosphorylation levels of spastin.
source: To validate whether staurosporine could decrease the phosphorylation levels of spastin, we enriched spastin through immunoprecipitation and used Pan phosphoserine/threonine antibody to observe spastin's phosphorylation. The results showed that staurosporine significantly reduces the phosphorylation levels of spastin (Figure 2D).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoprecipitation and western blot data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The presence of staurosporine markedly weakens the binding between spastin and 14-3-3.
source: Furthermore, our results revealed that the presence of staurosporine markedly weakened the binding between spastin and 14-3-3, indicating that phosphorylation of spastin is sufficient for the binding with 14-3-3 (Figure 2E).
evidence: The claim is supported by GST pulldown data with staurosporine treatment shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Phosphorylation of spastin is sufficient for the binding with 14-3-3.
source: Furthermore, our results revealed that the presence of staurosporine markedly weakened the binding between spastin and 14-3-3, indicating that phosphorylation of spastin is sufficient for the binding with 14-3-3 (Figure 2E).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the staurosporine experiment results shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Spastin S562A can bind with 14-3-3, while spastin S233A and spastin Pan A cannot.
source: Immunoprecipitation of the lysates, using an antibody against GFP, revealed that spastin S562A can bind with 14-3-3, while spastin S233A and spastin Pan A cannot (Figure 2G).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoprecipitation data with spastin mutants shown in Figure 2G.

claim: Spastin S233D exhibits enhanced binding to 14-3-3 compared to both wild-type and spastin S233A.
source: To further illustrate the significance of phosphorylation of spastin at S233 in its interaction with 14-3-3, the mutation of Ser233 in spastin to aspartic acid was also transfected for immunoprecipitation, the results revealed that spastin S233D exhibited enhanced binding to 14-3-3 compared to both wild-type and spastin S233A, and this interaction was even insensitive to the staurosporine treatment (Figure 2H).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoprecipitation data with spastin S233D mutant shown in Figure 2H.

claim: The interaction between spastin S233D and 14-3-3 is insensitive to staurosporine treatment.
source: To further illustrate the significance of phosphorylation of spastin at S233 in its interaction with 14-3-3, the mutation of Ser233 in spastin to aspartic acid was also transfected for immunoprecipitation, the results revealed that spastin S233D exhibited enhanced binding to 14-3-3 compared to both wild-type and spastin S233A, and this interaction was even insensitive to the staurosporine treatment (Figure 2H).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoprecipitation data with spastin S233D mutant and staurosporine treatment shown in Figure 2H.

claim: Both spastin S233A and S233D mutants effectively sever microtubules in COS7 cells.
source: Meanwhile, upon transfecting GFP-tagged spastin S233A and S233D mutants into COS7 cells, we observed that both spastin S233A and S233D mutants effectively severed microtubules, which indicates that the phosphorylation of the spastin S233 residue does not affect spastin's ability to sever microtubules (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by microtubule severing assays in COS7 cells shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The phosphorylation of the spastin S233 residue does not affect spastin's ability to sever microtubules.
source: Meanwhile, upon transfecting GFP-tagged spastin S233A and S233D mutants into COS7 cells, we observed that both spastin S233A and S233D mutants effectively severed microtubules, which indicates that the phosphorylation of the spastin S233 residue does not affect spastin's ability to sever microtubules (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that both S233A and S233D mutants sever microtubules effectively, shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Spastin promotes neurite outgrowth in hippocampal neurons.
source: Consistent with earlier results (Jiang et al., 2020; Riano et al., 2009), spastin promoted neurite outgrowth, as evidenced by both the length and branches of neurite.
evidence: The claim is supported by data from hippocampal neuron cultures and citations to Jiang et al., 2020; Riano et al., 2009.

claim: The promotion effect of spastin on neurite outgrowth is abolished when Ser233 is mutated to alanine.
source: However, the promotion effect of spastin on neurite outgrowth is abolished when Ser233 was mutated to alanine, whereas the promotion effect of spastin on neurite outgrowth is significantly enhanced when Ser233 was mutated to aspartic acid.
evidence: The claim is supported by neurite outgrowth data from hippocampal neurons transfected with spastin mutants shown in Figure 2I-K.

claim: The promotion effect of spastin on neurite outgrowth is significantly enhanced when Ser233 is mutated to aspartic acid.
source: However, the promotion effect of spastin on neurite outgrowth is abolished when Ser233 was mutated to alanine, whereas the promotion effect of spastin on neurite outgrowth is significantly enhanced when Ser233 was mutated to aspartic acid.
evidence: The claim is supported by neurite outgrowth data from hippocampal neurons transfected with spastin mutants shown in Figure 2I-K.

claim: The phosphorylation of Ser233 in spastin exerts a positive effect on neurite outgrowth during development.
source: These findings suggest that the phosphorylation of Ser233 in spastin exerts a positive effect on neurite outgrowth during development.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the neurite outgrowth experiments with spastin S233 mutants.

claim: Expression of GFP-spastin protein is markedly downregulated at 9 hr after cycloheximide (CHX) treatment.
source: Results showed that expression of GFP-spastin protein was markedly downregulated at 9 hr after CHX treatment (Figure 3A).
evidence: The claim is supported by western blot data from CHX chase experiments shown in Figure 3A.

claim: 14-3-3 can significantly protect spastin from degradation after CHX treatment, even after 12 hr.
source: Next, we co-expressed Flag-14-3-3 with GFP-spastin in the same treatment and found that 14-3-3 could significantly protect spastin from degradation after CHX treatment, even after 12 hr (Figure 3B).
evidence: The claim is supported by western blot data from CHX chase experiments with 14-3-3 co-expression shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Phosphorylation of spastin at S233 (S233D) protects spastin from degradation.
source: The results demonstrated that phosphorylation of spastin at S233 (S233D) protected spastin from degradation (Figure 3C&D&I).
evidence: The claim is supported by western blot data from CHX chase experiments with spastin S233D mutant shown in Figure 3C, D, and I.

claim: 14-3-3 can upregulate the protein levels of spastin.
source: Therefore, we conducted chase-time assays by overexpressing GFP-spastin without the addition of CHX. The results showed that 14-3-3 could upregulate the protein levels of spastin (Figure 3E&F&J).
evidence: The claim is supported by western blot data from time-course experiments with 14-3-3 co-expression shown in Figure 3E, F, and J.

claim: Spastin S233D significantly increases the protein level compared to wild-type spastin.
source: We also observed that spastin S233D significantly increased the protein level compared to the wild-type spastin (Figure 3G&K).
evidence: The claim is supported by western blot data from time-course experiments with spastin S233D mutant shown in Figure 3G and K.

claim: 14-3-3 can inhibit protein turnover by binding to phosphorylated spastin and upregulate the protein levels of spastin.
source: These findings suggest that 14-3-3 can inhibit protein turnover by binding to phosphorylated spastin and upregulate the protein levels of spastin.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the protein stability experiments shown in Figure 3.

claim: In the presence of MG132, the protein levels of spastin significantly increase in cortical neurons.
source: The results revealed that in the presence of MG132, the protein levels of spastin significantly increased. However, in the presence of CHX, the protein levels of spastin decreased, while the inhibition of ubiquitin-proteasome degradation by MG132 did not show a significant decrease (Figure 3L&M).
evidence: The claim is supported by western blot data from cortical neurons treated with MG132 and CHX shown in Figure 3L and M.

claim: There is a proteasomal degradation pathway for spastin.
source: These findings indicate the presence of a proteasomal degradation pathway for spastin.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the MG132 experiments shown in Figure 3L and M.

claim: FC-A can enhance the binding of 14-3-3/spastin.
source: We found that FC-A could enhance the binding of 14-3-3/spastin, as evidenced by more intense bands compared to no FC-A application, whereas R18 could efficiently inhibit the binding of 14-3-3/spastin with almost no binding was detected (Figure 4B).
evidence: The claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data with FC-A treatment shown in Figure 4B.

claim: R18 can efficiently inhibit the binding of 14-3-3/spastin.
source: We found that FC-A could enhance the binding of 14-3-3/spastin, as evidenced by more intense bands compared to no FC-A application, whereas R18 could efficiently inhibit the binding of 14-3-3/spastin with almost no binding was detected (Figure 4B).
evidence: The claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data with R18 treatment shown in Figure 4B.

claim: GFP-spastin can be ubiquitinated.
source: Results indicated that GFP-spastin could be ubiquitinated, while the ubiquitination of non-phosphorylated spastin (S233A) was significantly enhanced, and the addition of the 14-3-3 inhibitor R18 elevated the ubiquitination levels of spastin (Figure 3N&O).
evidence: The claim is supported by ubiquitination assay data shown in Figure 3N and O.

claim: The ubiquitination of non-phosphorylated spastin (S233A) is significantly enhanced compared to wild-type spastin.
source: Results indicated that GFP-spastin could be ubiquitinated, while the ubiquitination of non-phosphorylated spastin (S233A) was significantly enhanced, and the addition of the 14-3-3 inhibitor R18 elevated the ubiquitination levels of spastin (Figure 3N&O).
evidence: The claim is supported by ubiquitination assay data comparing wild-type and S233A mutant shown in Figure 3N and O.

claim: The addition of the 14-3-3 inhibitor R18 elevates the ubiquitination levels of spastin.
source: Results indicated that GFP-spastin could be ubiquitinated, while the ubiquitination of non-phosphorylated spastin (S233A) was significantly enhanced, and the addition of the 14-3-3 inhibitor R18 elevated the ubiquitination levels of spastin (Figure 3N&O).
evidence: The claim is supported by ubiquitination assay data with R18 treatment shown in Figure 3N and O.

claim: Cells transfected with wild-type spastin significantly induce microtubule severing in COS7 cells.
source: Results showed that cells transfected with wild-type spastin significantly induced microtubule severing, as evidenced by almost no MT staining (Figure 3P), while ubiquitin inhibited severing, leading to increased microtubule staining.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data from COS7 cells shown in Figure 3P.

claim: Ubiquitin inhibits spastin-mediated microtubule severing, leading to increased microtubule staining.
source: Results showed that cells transfected with wild-type spastin significantly induced microtubule severing, as evidenced by almost no MT staining (Figure 3P), while ubiquitin inhibited severing, leading to increased microtubule staining.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data from COS7 cells co-transfected with spastin and ubiquitin shown in Figure 3P.

claim: 14-3-3 upregulates microtubule severing mediated by spastin.
source: Based on these conditions, further transfection with 14-3-3 plasmid induced less microtubule staining, indicating that 14-3-3 upregulates microtubule severing and the process is mediated by spastin.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data from COS7 cells co-transfected with spastin, ubiquitin, and 14-3-3 shown in Figure 3P.

claim: 14-3-3 can upregulate the severing ability of spastin S233D, but not S233A.
source: Furthermore, we investigated whether this effect was dependent on spastin S233 phosphorylation by replacing GFP-spastin with GFP-spastin (S233A or S233D) during transfection. Results showed that 14-3-3 could upregulate the severing ability of spastin S233D, but not S233A (Figure 3Q, Figure 3—figure supplement 1), further indicating that 14-3-3 binds to the phosphorylation of S233 in spastin and promotes its microtubule severing ability.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data from COS7 cells with spastin S233 mutants shown in Figure 3Q and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: 14-3-3 binds to the phosphorylation of S233 in spastin and promotes its microtubule severing ability.
source: Furthermore, we investigated whether this effect was dependent on spastin S233 phosphorylation by replacing GFP-spastin with GFP-spastin (S233A or S233D) during transfection. Results showed that 14-3-3 could upregulate the severing ability of spastin S233D, but not S233A (Figure 3Q, Figure 3—figure supplement 1), further indicating that 14-3-3 binds to the phosphorylation of S233 in spastin and promotes its microtubule severing ability.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the microtubule severing experiments with spastin S233 mutants shown in Figure 3Q and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Glutamate induces neurite swelling and breakage in hippocampal neurons.
source: Our results showed that the injured neurons had numerous swellings and breakages on the neurite, indicative of successful establishment of an injury model (Figure 4C).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data from glutamate-treated hippocampal neurons shown in Figure 4C.

claim: FC-A can promote neurite outgrowth after glutamate-induced injury in hippocampal neurons.
source: Results demonstrated that FC-A could promote neurite outgrowth, both with regards to lengths and branches, after glutamate-induced injury, while this promoting effect was abolished following spastazoline administration (Figure 4D–G).
evidence: The claim is supported by neurite outgrowth data from glutamate-injured hippocampal neurons treated with FC-A shown in Figure 4D-G.

claim: The promoting effect of FC-A on neurite outgrowth after glutamate-induced injury is abolished following spastazoline administration.
source: Results demonstrated that FC-A could promote neurite outgrowth, both with regards to lengths and branches, after glutamate-induced injury, while this promoting effect was abolished following spastazoline administration (Figure 4D–G).
evidence: The claim is supported by neurite outgrowth data from glutamate-injured hippocampal neurons treated with FC-A and spastazoline shown in Figure 4D-G.

claim: Transfection of R18 results in an inhibitory effect on neurite outgrowth after injury.
source: In contrast, transfection of R18 resulted in an inhibitory effect on neurite outgrowth, but this was rescued with moderate spastin expression after injury (Figure 4D–J).
evidence: The claim is supported by neurite outgrowth data from injured hippocampal neurons transfected with R18 shown in Figure 4D-J.
